item.title: How to Migrate n8n from npm to Docker Before n8n 3.0
item.description:
Introduction

If you run n8n from npx n8n or a global npm install n8n -g, your installation has an expiry date. n8n 3.0, scheduled for October 2026, drops support for npm-based installs entirely, and the n8n package on npm stops at the last 2.x release. This guide migrates a working npm install to Docker Compose without losing workflows, credentials, or execution history. It is written for self-hosters on a VPS or home server who installed n8n the quick way years ago and now need the supported path. If you followed our Ubuntu VPS install guide, the backup habits from that post apply here too.

item.title: n8n 3.0 Upgrade Guide: The Breaking Changes Checklist Before You Update
item.description:
Introduction

n8n 3.0, scheduled for October 2026, is the most disruptive release in the project’s recent history. It ends npm and npx installs for self-hosters, removes more than 35 legacy nodes and helpers, retires Chat Hub, and tightens security defaults that change how Code nodes, community packages, and webhooks behave. This guide is the pre-upgrade checklist for anyone running a production 2.x instance, on Docker or npm, who owns workflows that must keep working the morning after the upgrade. If you have not yet moved off npm, read our npm to Docker migration guide alongside this one, because that move is now mandatory.

item.title: MCP Stateless Spec Migration Guide: Move Your Server to 2026-07-28 Without Downtime
item.description:
Introduction

If you run an MCP server built on the 2025-era Streamable HTTP transport, your request lifecycle starts with an initialize handshake and depends on a sticky Mcp-Session-Id header for everything that follows. On 28 July 2026 the Model Context Protocol shipped revision 2026-07-28, which deletes both of those concepts and makes every request self-describing. MCP co-creator David Soria Parra calls it “[MCP’s] most important [release] since remote MCP first launched.” This guide migrates your server to the new stateless wire: what to delete, what to implement (server/discover, per-request _meta, the new headers), how to keep 2025-era clients working during the transition, and how to regression-test the whole thing. It is written for developers who already operate an MCP server over Streamable HTTP. If you have never built one, start with our Model Context Protocol pillar guide first.

item.title: How to Migrate from Zapier to n8n
item.description:
Quick answer

How do I migrate from Zapier to n8n? There is no automatic importer, you rebuild each Zap as an n8n workflow, mapping Zapier triggers to n8n trigger nodes and actions to n8n nodes. Inventory your Zaps, export what you can, rebuild one workflow at a time starting with the simplest, reconnect your app credentials in n8n, test with real data, then switch off the Zap.

Introduction

The most common reason people migrate from Zapier to n8n is the bill. Zapier charges per task, every successful action step in a Zap counts separately, so costs grow with both volume and complexity. n8n charges per execution: one workflow run counts as one execution whether the workflow has 3 nodes or 30. A 5-action Zap firing 1,000 times a month consumes 5,000 Zapier tasks but only 1,000 n8n executions. On self-hosted n8n, it consumes nothing at all beyond the server you already pay for.
